transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

I keep forgetting everyday things like appointments and errands, and it’s starting to really mess up taking care of my wife and my commitments in the garden project. I just feel so overwhelmed trying to keep track of everything lately, and it's causing a lot of trouble at home.
Along with these memory issues, have you been feeling persistently down, sad, or lost interest in activities you usually enjoy, like your gardening?

No, I don't feel sad or down, and I definitely haven't lost interest in gardening or my other hobbies. I still really want to do them, but I just get so easily distracted and overwhelmed that I can't stay organized enough to follow through.
Are you still able to manage your daily tasks, like handling finances or medications, on your own, or do you now need help from others to get them done?

I'm trying to handle everything on my own since my wife's stroke, but I am really struggling to do it reliably. I keep messing up the bills and insurance forms, forgetting her prescriptions, and even wandering off halfway through sorting her weekly medications. It's incredibly frustrating because my wife can't fully rely on me for these crucial tasks right now, and it's causing a lot of tension.
Are you still able to eventually complete these tasks like paying bills and managing medications on your own, or has it gotten to the point where someone else must take over and do them for you?

No, nobody else has taken over because my wife isn't able to do them, so I am still the one responsible. But I'm struggling terribly to get them done right, often leaving her medications half-sorted or messing up the insurance paperwork. It's causing a lot of tension because she feels she can't safely rely on me to finish these critical tasks.
Have you recently had any physical illnesses, head injuries, or other medical conditions that started around the same time as these memory problems?

No, I haven't had any head injuries or illnesses myself, and I'm actually physically quite well. These planning and memory struggles really became overwhelming about 14 months ago when my wife had a stroke and I had to take on all of her care and scheduling. It was the sudden increase in responsibilities that brought these issues to light, rather than any medical problem of my own.
Are you still able to handle your own personal daily care, such as bathing, dressing, and eating, entirely on your own without any difficulty?

Oh, yes, I have absolutely no trouble with bathing, dressing, or eating on my own. Physically I'm doing just fine, and my struggles are strictly with organizing schedules, handling paperwork, and keeping track of appointments. It's the planning and remembering that I can't seem to manage, not my basic personal care.

While you are struggling with your wife's complex care, are you still able to manage your own personal affairs—like your own doctor visits, medications, and money—without making mistakes that put your own well-being at risk?

To be honest, my own affairs are suffering just as much. While I'm physically healthy and don't have many medical needs of my own, I've been messing up our household bills and missing my own appointments because of my forgetfulness. It's definitely putting our financial and personal organization at risk.
Have you noticed that these difficulties with your memory and organization have been gradually getting worse over the past 14 months, or have they stayed at about the same level?

I’ve actually had these tendencies to be easily distracted and restless my whole life, but they became a major, constant struggle about 14 months ago when my wife had her stroke. Since taking on all her care and paperwork, the level of difficulty and overwhelm has stayed consistently high and disruptive. The demands have remained heavy, so it has been a constant struggle since then.

You mentioned having these tendencies to be easily distracted and restless your whole life. Did you experience these same difficulties with attention, organization, or sitting still during your childhood or school years?

Yes, they definitely go back to my childhood. Even in primary school, my teachers frequently complained to my parents that I couldn't sit still and talked out of turn constantly. I would also leave my worksheets half-finished because I'd completely lose track of what we were supposed to be doing.
Do you still experience restlessness, difficulty sitting still, or a tendency to act or speak impulsively in your day-to-day life now?

Yes, I absolutely still struggle with that. I constantly feel a jumpy energy in my body, especially when I have to sit still in waiting rooms or wait in lines at the pharmacy, which makes me incredibly fidgety and impatient. I also find myself blurting out answers and cutting people off in conversations before they even finish what they are saying.

While the functional impairment became more pronounced 14 months ago due to the increased cognitive demands of caregiving after his wife's stroke, the symptoms themselves are chronic and not due to a progressive cognitive decline or a mood disorder. The clinical picture is highly consistent with Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ICD-10: F90.0), and no further testing is required to make this diagnosis.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong history of severe inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity dating back to early childhood (primary school). While he managed to cope for many years, his coping mechanisms were overwhelmed 14 months ago when his wife's stroke drastically increased his cognitive load and administrative responsibilities. He meets full criteria for ADHD, combined presentation (ICD-10 F90.0), as evidenced by persistent difficulties with organization, distractibility, forgetfulness, physical restlessness, and verbal impulsivity that cause significant functional impairment in his daily caregiving and household management.
